idiom_name: Sequence.makeIterator() + IteratorProtocol.next() -> Element? driven by for-in
implementation_notes: Swift models the pattern as two standard-library protocols: the aggregate conforms to Sequence by implementing makeIterator(), the iterator conforms to IteratorProtocol with a single mutating next() -> Element? returning nil at the end, and for-in drives exactly that pair, so the classic classes disappear into protocol conformance. Conform to the more constrained Collection protocol when the type supports non-destructive multi-pass iteration (count, indices, random access) - a plain Sequence makes no such promise and may be destructively consumed. Write a custom iterator for non-collection sources (streams, generators, linked structures) and prefer lazy views (lazy.map/lazy.filter) over building intermediate arrays.
pitfalls: IteratorProtocol conformers are value types: copying an iterator copies its cursor, and advancing one copy may invalidate the other (the documentation warns explicitly), so iterators must be obtained from makeIterator() rather than copied.
A Sequence makes no re-iteration promise: two for-in loops over a non-Collection sequence may not restart, so algorithms needing multiple passes must require Collection.
next() is mutating; keeping an iterator in a class to share it invites interleaved advancement, and a Sequence that is also its own iterator is single-pass by construction.

variants.name: AsyncSequence with for await
variants.idiom_name: AsyncSequence.makeAsyncIterator() + async next(), consumed by for await-in
variants.implementation_notes: Swift 5.5's structured concurrency adds the asynchronous counterpart: a type conforms to AsyncSequence by providing makeAsyncIterator(), its iterator conforms to AsyncIteratorProtocol whose next() is async and may throw, and for-await-in awaits each element - the same shape as IteratorProtocol with a suspension point per step. AsyncStream/AsyncThrowingStream adapt callback APIs (yield from a continuation, onTermination for cleanup), and the loop participates in task cancellation. Use it for time-based or IO-driven sources (notifications, byte streams, sensor feeds); keep the synchronous Sequence for in-memory data.
pitfalls: Every next() suspends, so the iterator's state spans suspension points: ad-hoc concurrent calls to next() on one iterator are a data race, and the iterator must be safe to send across isolation domains.
for-await obeys task cancellation: the loop ends early and the sequence's termination handler runs, so code that assumes a full traversal must handle partial results.
AsyncStream's buffering policy decides whether a slow consumer drops elements or stalls producers, and forgetting onTermination leaks the underlying monitor/subscription.
